articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Bosses from Great Britain’s biggest energy companies called to meeting as part of government’s debt relief plan
An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends almost £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts.
Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Minister tells energy suppliers to do more to help households tackle unpaid bills this winter

articles.author: Harriet Grant
articles.description:
As new pornography laws come into force, officers say viewing extreme content could lead young people towards abuse images
Police forces are turning to specialist charities and partner agencies to cope with the growing number of teenagers caught up in online child abuse.
As new pornography laws come into force, frontline officers warn that young people are going down a pathway through extreme content that could lead to real-life abusive images of children.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police turn to charities for help with teenagers caught up in online child abuse

articles.author: Adam Fulton (now); Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Kirsty McEwen, Lucy Campbell, Taz Ali and Jonathan Yerushalmy (earlier)
articles.description:
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats, including in Ohio, Arizona and North Carolina; Ted Cruz calls election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’ 

Live results | Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win

Sign up for Breaking News US email

Election night brought a series of dramatic developments, unexpected results and closely contested races across the US. We have put together this video capturing the key moments and offering a quick overview of one of the most important nights in US politics:
The Senate race in Mississippi has become one of the most closely watched contests in the midterms, with Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom separated by a remarkably narrow margin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats exceed 250 House seats as blue wave sweeping Congress grows

articles.author: Ima Caldwell and Kat Wong
articles.description:
Former NSW police officer gives evidence for a second day after pleading not guilty to murdering Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024

Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: former police officer continues evidence in double murder trial

Beau Lamarre-Condon “stands by” his decision to shoot Jesse Baird but did not intend to kill him, the New South Wales supreme court has heard.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon tells double murder trial shooting of Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional but ‘it was my fault’

articles.author: Tom McIlroy and Patrick Commins
articles.description:
Anthony Albanese’s government has taken a blow due to Iran war but voter anxiety around cost of living and datacentres may hit harder

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Democrats’ stunning midterm victory should broaden Australia’s alliance with the US, observers say, even as a new power base emerges in Washington, affecting Aukus, datacentre development and relations with China.
Cabinet ministers, diplomats and Australia’s defence industrial sector closely watched the results this week, with control of the US Congress flipping to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years in office badly dinted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia faces same issues that flipped control of US Congress in midterms, experts say

articles.author: Penry Buckley NSW state reporter
articles.description:
Eva Geller was shot on 14 December 2025 during Hanukah festival and had been in and out of hospital since

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast


A woman who was shot during the Bondi beach terror attack has died in hospital almost 12 months after the massacre.
Eva Geller, 90, had been in and out of hospital this year for treatment of injuries sustained during the attack on 14 December, a senior Jewish community source said on Friday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bondi beach shooting: Eva Geller, 90, shot during massacre dies in hospital year after antisemitic attack

articles.author: Kat Wong
articles.description:
This blog has now closed

Beau Lamarre-Condon tells double murder trial shooting of Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional but ‘it was my fault’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Lamarre-Condon tells the court he had seen what he assumed to be someone’s delivery motorcycle:
As soon as I saw that I had an idea … I saw a hi-vis hooded jacket, waterproof long pants and gloves.
This moment here … I wish that I didn’t do this … But I had the thought process that if I was to put on this helmet and outfit I could knock on Jesse’s door I would look like an UberEats driver without any verbal interaction with Jesse.
At the very least I would have had an AVO out against me … police don’t hesitate to put another police on an AVO … I was worried if I knocked on the door it would be perceived as harassment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial: prosecution begins cross-examination of double murder accused – as it happened

articles.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
articles.description:
Opposition leader Jess Wilson grimaces as the ‘Jess Express’, carrying Liberals and reporters, backs into the structure in suburban Melbourne

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Liberal party’s first offical day on the campaign trail has hit a snag, after its campaign bus reversed into the awning of a shopfront.
The “Jess Express”, a large blue bus emblazoned with an image of the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, was unveiled on Friday, 12 days after Labor launched its own red equivalent.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Liberal bus crashes into shop awning on its first outing of Victorian election campaign

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
President seeks to make Oval Office a national monument to ensure designs are not ‘ripped down by stupid people’
Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.
In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump signs proclamation to try to prevent changes to gold-covered Oval Office

articles.author: Guardian staff and agency
articles.description:
Unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day previously happened in 2010
Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.
In a record-tying 19th execution of the year, Florida executed Jesse Guardado via a three-drug lethal injection. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton county home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Alabama, Florida and Indiana carry out executions on same day

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
Mark Rowley calls for ‘revolution’ in policing as major review is expected to propose regional ‘super forces’
Police are heading for failure unless the number of forces in England and Wales is slashed, with their ability to catch criminals collapsing and public confidence falling, Britain’s top officer will say on Friday.
The stark comments from Sir Mark Rowley, the commissioner of the Metropolitan police, come as some police leaders demand a radical package of reforms.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Slashing number of police forces in England and Wales is only option, says Met chief

articles.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
articles.description:
News channel trailed NBC and ABC, but edged out CNN, MS Now and CBS in primetime hours on midterm election night

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

On a midterm election night that was a huge disappointment for Republicans, with Democrats taking control of the US House and Senate, the country’s most prominent conservative television network seemingly felt the brunt of viewer disillusionment with Donald Trump and his party, according to final audience numbers released on Thursday.
The Fox News channel, which often leads among all news networks in viewership on election nights, fell behind two top broadcasters on Tuesday. According to ratings dating from the Nielsen firm, the network averaged 4.3 million total viewers between 8 and 11pm, behind broadcast networks NBC (6.7 million viewers) and ABC (5.2 million viewers), though it edged out fellow cable networks CNN (4.1 million viewers) and MS Now (3.7 million viewers). Fox News handedly defeat CBS News, which attracted just 2.8 million viewers. CNN performed better in the 25-to-54 age demographic prized by advertisers, besting Fox News, MS Now and CBS.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fox News suffers ratings drop on bleak election night for Republicans

articles.author: Auzzy Byrdsell in New York City
articles.description:
Website known for politics, arts and culture coverage announces closure just weeks before anniversary
Salon, one of the early internet’s pioneering publications, is closing after more than three decades, the outlet announced on Thursday.
“It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website,” Salon said in a statement. “It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Salon, internet’s oldest general interest publication, shuts down after 31 years

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.
The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.
 
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz and Geraldine McKelvie
articles.description:
Detective urges other potential victims to come forward and says: ‘Our work’s not done’
The lead detective in the case against Russell Brand has urged other potential victims of the comedian to come forward after it emerged he is under investigation for two further rape allegations and faces a civil claim in the UK.
Det Supt Andy Furphy, the Metropolitan police’s strategic lead in the investigation, described Brand, 51, as “a predator” whose behaviour escalated as his fame grew.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police investigating two further rape allegations against Russell Brand

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse
Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.
At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis

articles.author: Rory Carroll in Dublin, Gwyn Topham, Jakub Krupa and Dan Sabbagh in London
articles.description:
Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel

Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

Hoax bomb threats have disrupted at least 34 flights across Europe this week, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.
At least 25 bomb threats affected flights on Thursday between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bomb threats disrupt dozens of flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears

articles.author: Jason Burke International security correspondent and agencies
articles.description:
President says he will make a decision on Sunday about who should try to build a government as Netanyahu rival is endorsed by 67 lawmakers 
Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.
Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had ​endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results ‌of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the ‌best shot to form a government.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel’s Herzog yet to decide on who should form government as Eisenkot secures significant backing

articles.author: Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
EU transport commissioner says ‘too early’ to say if bomb threats to 20 flights are linked

Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats?

And the Italian news agency Ansa reported that two more planes with links to Italy were affected by bomb threats this morning: that’s a WizzAir service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw, which reportedly landed in Vienna, and a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome Fiumicino.
Belgian newspaper Le Soir also reported a bomb threat against a LOT Polish Airline flight from Warsaw, which now landed at Zaventem.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Multiple planes diverted as bomb threats to commercial flights reported across Europe – as it happened

articles.author: Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect
The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry

articles.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
articles.description:
Hundreds of thousands demonstrate over cost of living and cuts to public services as 70,000 police officers deployed
Hundreds of thousands of people have marched in cities across France in the latest round of street demonstrations, as trade unions put pressure on the government with a general strike over the cost of living and cuts to public services.
Striking teachers, hospital staff and rail workers joined high school and university students in largely peaceful demonstrations in Paris and other cities on Thursday amid a high police presence of 70,000 officers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Protesters march in cities across France as unions stage general strike

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign
Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said travelling overseas for procedures can end in infections, disfigurement and death.
Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, said travelling to countries such as Turkey for surgery came with myriad risks – and not just on the operating table.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beware ‘sun, sea and surgery’ cosmetic tourism packages, experts advise

articles.author: Owen Myers
articles.description:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors
The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.
A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say

UK politics live – latest updates

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power
The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.
A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war

articles.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Older voters praised for helping tip balance in leftwing president’s favour against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff
It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.
But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How elderly ‘unsung heroes’ powered Lula’s historic fightback in Brazil

articles.author: Danny Vincent in Hong Kong
articles.description:
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison

The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior staff correspondent
articles.description:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification 
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI

articles.author: Agencies
articles.description:
Seoul to seek parliamentary approval to extend anti-piracy Cheonghae unit’s area to about 650km from the vital strait after criticism from Donald Trump on Iran war support
South Korea plans to expand the operations ⁠of its anti-piracy unit to waters closer to the strait of Hormuz, its defence ministry has said, after pressure from Donald Trump to ⁠provide support for his war in Iran.
The government is to submit a motion to parliament that would expand the Cheonghae unit’s area of operation to waters near the port of Duqm in Oman, which ​is about 650km (403 miles) away from the strait. The motion also needs to be approved by ‌President Lee Jae Myung and the cabinet.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South Korea says it will expand naval operations closer to strait of Hormuz

articles.author: Ben Doherty
articles.description:
Analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo shows 85 of 132 shipments over eight years contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Millions of dollars of food grown in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled as “produce of Israel”, a new analysis of trade data has shown.
The human rights legal organisation Global Echo has analysed commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics, showing at least US$5m (A$7.2m) of organic dates grown in illegal settlements across the West Bank have been shipped to Australia over the past eight years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Food grown in illegal West Bank settlements being sold in Australia as ‘produce of Israel’

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
Conservation officers say more than one bear may have been involved in attack on women near their home
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mother and daughter killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm

articles.author: Alice Speri
articles.description:
Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Track live results from all 50 states

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.
Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Iran celebrates its claimed role in ‘regime change’ amid pressure on Trump to ‘finish the job’ with attack

US midterms live – latest updates

Iran this week unveiled a huge billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.
The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran unveils ‘We will kill Trump’ banner – but US president may now be tempted to resume bombing

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
The incident took place in the same province where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren last November
A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.
On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One dead and another missing in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
articles.description:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.
Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Durban Deep
articles.description:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
The Democrats have gained new powers to constrain Donald Trump. But the drubbing that Republicans received could yet prompt him to new excesses
Donald Trump is a president without parallel, but history can still be instructive. Lame duck presidents often focus on foreign policy to escape domestic discontent and establish a legacy in an area where a hostile Congress offers less of an obstacle. Mr Trump, who was stunningly rebuffed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms, might seek satisfaction in construction projects, the 2028 presidential race and his family’s future. Or, amid the humiliation and with Republican critics growing louder, he could distract attention with fresh adventurism – perhaps escalating against Cuba – or more likely a vengeful new offensive against Iran.
Mr Trump won’t put in the legwork or attention to detail demanded by, say, Bill Clinton’s push for lasting peace in the Middle East. But he loves the glitz of state visits, spectacular military action, hobnobbing with strongmen and (unearned) credit for dubious “peace deals”. With a potential three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping mooted for the Apec summit in China this month, Ukraine, Taiwan and others have reason to be nervous.

An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.
Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

articles.author: Jon Henley and Senay Boztas in Amsterdam
articles.description:
In the Netherlands many felt the move, while welcome, was mishandled and exclusionary, mirroring past inequality
Andy Burnham’s pledge to seek a “structured dialogue” with former colonies to help shape Britain’s first formal state apology for slavery marks the UK’s first tentative step down a path the Netherlands set out on five years ago.
The prime minister’s attempts to initiate a historic shift alongside the royal family – whose customary expressions of “profound personal sorrow”, falling short of an apology, was repeated by King Charles this week – echo a process begun by the Dutch state in 2021.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What can Britain learn from backlash to Dutch slavery apology?

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin
articles.description:
Debate has focused on cash payments, but advocates say reparatory justice must address much more than money
The debate in much of the British media over reparations has focused almost entirely on cash payments: how much Britain might owe for its role in transatlantic enslavement, who should pay and whether people today should be held responsible for the actions of those who came before them.
But some campaigners warn that this narrow focus overlooks the broader goals of the reparations movement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Repairing the legacy of slavery: what are campaigners calling for?

articles.author: Sandra Laville
articles.description:
With parts of region served by company in severe drought still, regulators give it six weeks to come up with action plan
Repeated failures by South West Water to tackle leaks are putting customers at higher risks of losing water supplies as parts of the region remain in severe drought, regulators have said.
In a warning to the privatised company that serves 1.8 million people across the south-west of England, the regulators said it had been failing to meet targets to reduce leaks and repair burst pipes for seven years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South West Water’s failure to fix leaks ‘putting customer supplies at risk’

articles.author: Lauren Almeida and agencies
articles.description:
Gordon Brothers still in ‘active discussions’ with interested parties and seeking to ‘protect as many jobs as possible’
The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of its handling of the retailer.
Gordon Brothers said on Thursday morning that it was still in “active discussions” with interested suitors and had been seeking to “protect as many jobs as possible”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Poundland’s US owner says retailer remains ‘vulnerable’, after talks with ministers

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Consultation led by Department for Transport will consider parking standards, fleet sizes and insurance requirements
Ministers are seeking to end the “wild west” of parked ebikes blocking pavements, as they attempt to crack down on antisocial behaviour such as cyclists jumping red lights.
The consultation, led by the Department for Transport, will aim to establish national standards on issues including parking, ending the current patchwork of agreements between individual bike companies and councils.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ministers to target ‘wild west’ of ebikes blocking pavements

articles.author: Karen McVeigh
articles.description:
Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050
Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.
Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
William the Conqueror-built Hastings Castle and Swiss-style writing retreat in Kent two of nearly 200 additions to list
A castle built by William the Conqueror, a Swiss-style chalet where Charles Dickens wrote and a swathe of fire-blasted moorland are among sites that have been added to Historic England’s heritage at risk register.
Almost 200 historic places have been added to the already extensive list, including Hastings Castle in East Sussex, Dickens’ wooden writing retreat in Kent and Fylingdales Moor in North Yorkshire, which was devastated by a wildfire in the summer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Norman conquest castle and Dickens chalet among sites added to heritage at risk register

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior staff correspondent
articles.description:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification 
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Controversial theory that Verica, who incited Emperor Claudius’s AD43 landing, was a woman could put a new spin on British history if true
It was a moment that changed the course of British history: in AD43, Roman troops under the emperor Claudius landed in Kent. Now, an archaeologist has claimed the British ruler who persuaded Claudius to invade was not a king but a queen.
The controversial conclusion, made by Dr Miles Russell, the director of archaeological fieldwork at Bournemouth University, could throw new light on Britain’s history.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK

articles.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
Fleabag creator joins stars signing up to scheme aimed at tackling class barriers in theatre
Phoebe Waller-Bridge has donated a London flat so that early-career writers can afford to live in the capital.
The creator of the hit show Fleabag bought the property specifically for Writers’ Block, a new scheme tackling class barriers in theatre. The flat will be offered to writers from disadvantaged backgrounds, who will pay only bills. Waller-Bridge has also made what the initiative described as a “generous financial contribution”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Phoebe Waller-Bridge donates flat to help early-career writers live in London

articles.author: Joe Pinner
articles.description:
Ministers urged to go further than proposed cut to 110 decibels to ease acute stress on birds and other animals
Campaigners are calling on the UK government to protect the welfare of wild animals by cutting the maximum noise level of fireworks sold to the public from 120 to 90 decibels.
The Center for Wild Animal Welfare (CWAW) has said lowering the limit to 90dB – which is about one-eighth of the loudness of 120dB – would help to protect millions of wild animals from acute stress by reducing the area over which a firework disturbs surrounding wildlife.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Firework noise limit should be drastically cut to protect wild animals, UK government told

articles.description:
King Charles addressed country leaders at the opening ceremony of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting, calling the transatlantic slave trade a 'shameful chapter of history … that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow'. Speaking in Antigua and Barbuda, the king said the slave trade 'still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth', but his remarks stopped short of an apology. Charles spoke just days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he was open to making a formal apology, although he has rejected calls for the UK to pay reparations


King Charles addresses summit as campaigners intensify demands for apology for slavery

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'Shameful chapter': King Charles stops short of slavery apology in Commonwealth speech – video

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
Nations in the group fare worse than others, with funding for nature projects especially hard hit even as climate crisis intensifies global need
The UK government has slashed overseas aid to Commonwealth countries, the Guardian can reveal, in contrast to the warm words for the group from King Charles and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, this week.
Amid sharp cuts in the UK’s aid budget overall, the Commonwealth has fared poorly, an analysis of the most recent and projected aid figures, seen by the Guardian, has shown.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK makes huge aid cuts to Commonwealth nations despite warm words at Chogm

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
British Veterinary Association president tells MPs surge in cases putting farmers under severe pressure and stress
The worst bluetongue season on record has been a major animal welfare crisis in Great Britain, MPs have been told, putting farmers under “severe emotional stress”.
Bluetongue, a viral disease that affects sheep, cattle and goats, can cause fever, lesions, stillbirths and death. The tongue may go blue and protrude from the mouth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Great Britain’s worst-ever bluetongue season ‘a major animal welfare crisis’

articles.author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
articles.description:
Hope Haven in Whitehaven is one of six trial open-access, 24/7 schemes in England offering preventive care
The night Tamara first walked through the doors of Hope Haven, a new community mental health hub in the heart of Whitehaven, she was afraid. “Terrified, actually,” she says. “Like, my life was falling apart. I didn’t know how to stop it from hurting.”
The 22-year-old, who works in children’s transport, had been in and out of therapy and counselling since she was 14, after being abused by an acquaintance as a child. After a lengthy legal process her abuser was sentenced, but the “mental challenge” of dealing with what had happened to her was not over.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘This is direct’: positive early feedback from pilot community mental health hub in Cumbria

articles.description:
Shabana Mahmood addressed the Commons to outline a revised set of proposals to the UK's legal migration system, softening plans to force low-paid workers to wait 15 years before settlement that resulted in a backlash from fellow cabinet ministers and backbench Labour MPs. Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary's policy would  now allow up to 300,000 people to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years

UK politics live – latest updates

Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shabana Mahmood sets out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants – video

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey, produced by Madelynne Flack, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
As home secretary Shabana Mahmood announces her controversial migration plans, Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey discuss the political context that has led to this announcement and why the timing for Andy Burnham – who is out of the country – is very convenient for him

You can watch Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why is Labour risking a row over migration? – podcast

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith, executive producers Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale.
articles.description:
What if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, Brexit, levelling up – and still failed to increase growth per person in the UK. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode of Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty, rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
You can watch previous episodes of Radical Thinking here
  

  
Aditya’s suggested reading list for this episode:
 

 

 As we say in the podcast, I’ve championed the work of Karel and Sukhdev and their colleagues for many years in the Guardian, and some of my columns are a good introduction to their approach.
In our conversation we look at what life after growth looks like for towns and suburbs, and what it should look like. This report from south Wales in 2016 examines the present-day reality.
For a broader analysis of how the UK has become highly unequal and increasingly stagnant, try this.
As part of the Foundational Economy Collective, Williams and Johal put a lot of their analysis into freely available working papers. That circumvents the leisureliness and expense of academic publishing and gets their arguments in front of a wider public. A good example is this one on the cost of living crisis.
More recently, they’ve focused on the broken water system of England and Wales in a book called Murky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast

articles.author: Sarah Marsh
articles.description:
From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them

What the budget means for you

Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I earn £126,000 – but nothing’s left at the end of the month’: readers react to the budget

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Teesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductive
“It’s disappointing, it’s just another kicking,” said a youth worker after the town in which they work was labelled as the hardest place in which to be a child in England.
“It suggests our children are living unhappy lives,” said a teacher, who described her pupils as joyful.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ label

articles.author: Esther Addley
articles.description:
Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It should never be forgotten’: families recount care home victims’ experiences in wake of Covid findings

articles.author: Graeme Wearden in London and Lauren Aratani in New York
articles.description:
Nearly $2tn shaved off Nasdaq value as worries of curbs to AI datacenters ripple across bourses
The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 18 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm election results.
As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into “correction territory” – more than 10% below its recent record high – with more than $2tn shaved off its value by the end of trading Thursday. The tech-heavy index had its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his “liberation day” tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nasdaq sees worst day in 18 months as investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats’ election triumph

articles.author: Emma Loffhagen
articles.description:
Philippe Jaenada told French radio that he used ChatGPT to ‘play with the reader’, after the prize removed a different book from its longlist over allegations of AI use
The winner of France’s most prestigious literary prize has admitted using artificial intelligence while writing his novel, barely a day after collecting an award whose jury had thrown out another book over suspected AI use.
Philippe Jaenada, who won the Prix Goncourt on Tuesday for L’Inconnue du quai de Javel (The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel), told France Inter radio on Wednesday that he had turned to AI “three times” while writing it.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Winner of the Prix Goncourt literary prize admits to using AI

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Minister hints at restriction on selling technology ‘to certain users’ amid worries over surreptitious filming of women

The government is considering placing restrictions on smart glasses amid concerns the technology is being used to surreptitiously film women, a minister has said.
Speaking in the House of Commons, the safeguarding minister, Satvir Kaur, hinted at a ban on selling the technology “to certain users”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK government considers smart glasses ban over secret filming concerns

articles.author: Charlie Allenby
articles.description:
What do you get the man who doesn’t seem to want anything? From fiery condiments to chef’s knives, slippers to portable speakers, these ideas are sure to hit the spot
• The best Christmas gifts for mums in 2026
Gifts for dads, grandads and other father figures can often feel like a shot in the dark. What do you get for someone who doesn’t seem to want anything, or who already has it all?
Shared experiences or promises of peace and quiet are popular options, but they are tricky to wrap. Which is where my recommendations come in.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The best Christmas gifts in the UK for dads, grandads, uncles and friends – tested for 2026

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman and Kai Wright with Blake Montgomery . Produced by Anabel Bacon and Monica Espitia, engineered by Ivan Kuraev, executive producer Rachel Humphreys
articles.description:
The tech industry spent big on the midterms, but it turned out to be a poor investment. Elon Musk poured a staggering $446m dollars into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, but his efforts didn’t pay off. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. Carter Sherman and Kai Wright are joined by the Guardian’s US tech editor, Blake Montgomery, to ask what the ‘blue tsunami’ will mean for Musk and the wider tech industry. Will this spell the end of AI datacenters? And if so, what could this mean for the US economy?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Was Elon Musk the US midterms' biggest loser? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
As GTA 6 looms, we look at the films that have influenced Rockstar’s creatives, from Heat to Bonnie and Clyde, via Boyz n the Hood and Speed
Grand Theft Auto is arguably the most cinematic video game series ever made. Over the past three decades, the games have studied and stolen the themes, conventions and visual dynamism of great gangster and action movies, applying them to open worlds filled with low-life characters and grand set-piece possibilities. Here then are the movies (and TV show) that have shaped the GTA experience, from the 1996 original to this year’s inescapable instalment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

articles.author: Blake Montgomery
articles.description:
Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult
The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.
The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
More than 100 campaign groups will join together in 15 countries this week to call for a halt to major AI projects
Protesters across Europe are planning two days of action against datacentres this week with demonstrations taking place in 15 countries.
More than 100 groups are joining together for the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday. They are calling for a moratorium on large projects, citing environmental and social costs that “we can no longer afford”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Activists across Europe prepare two days of protests against datacentres

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
All-round upgrades fit a bigger OLED screen in a smaller and lighter body with water resistance for first time
The new iPad mini takes Apple’s fan-favourite tiny tablet and upgrades just about everything about it, including giving it a new OLED screen, serious performance, speakers embedded into the display and even water resistance, all with a big new price tag.
The eighth-generation iPad mini costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099), which is £200 or equivalent more than the original price of its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to bite. That makes it uncomfortably expensive, costing £270 more than the base model iPad (A16) and only £50 cheaper than the bigger 11in iPad Air M4.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple iPad mini A20 Pro review: the best small tablet but with a big price

Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification 
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI

articles.author: Nick Robins-Early
articles.description:
The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates
Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment.
The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Owners of pilates and yoga studios in the US got political and encouraged their followers to vote on social media

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Track live results from all 50 states

Your local pilates instructors only want you to do two things: breathe through your side-planks and vote.
In the days leading up to the US midterm elections, a wave of posts from fitness and wellness accounts blanketed Instagram, eschewing their typical messaging around the importance of strengthening your core in favor of the importance of exercising your civic duty. Owners of pilates and yoga studios and instructors across the US posted reels and pictures on platforms like Instagram encouraging their followers and clients to vote. Engagement varied depending on their following: posts reaped anywhere from 70 to more than 10,000 likes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Wellness is on the ballot’: why did so many pilates studios tell me to vote in the midterms?

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court. It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths.
At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish. I began to wonder if my meds were making me hallucinate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

articles.author: Jon Henley in Paris
articles.description:
Temperature and defrosting thresholds raised to ‘very high levels’ at three cold stores stocking vital blood products
France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.
The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe

articles.author: Phoebe Davis and Daniel Boffey
articles.description:
Documents show Home Office developing programme to use technology for general immigration enforcement
The Home Office is preparing to deploy facial recognition technology at transport hubs and public events as part of the biggest immigration enforcement crackdown in British history.
Policy documents show the government has been developing a programme to deploy live facial recognition (LFR) cameras for “general immigration enforcement”, including non-criminal immigration offences.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK to deploy facial recognition in biggest-ever immigration crackdown

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo
This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains
It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time.
Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Firm reveals details about how its cryptocurrency exchange was compromised, saying operation began in June
The hackers behind the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance heist used bogus job interviews, malicious software and an internal AI tool, the company has revealed.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange was compromised in an operation that began with an inadvertent download of malware in June, led to a recruitment scam in September and then a raid last week of “hot wallets” where billions of dollars worth of crypto-assets were taken.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’

articles.author: Jane Hoskyn
articles.description:
Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season
• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Autumn, we’ve been expecting you. After a September that seemed to miss the memo about changing seasons, October made up for it with serial storms and nights that drew in faster than you could say “fall back”. Time to hunker down and, whisper it, even put the heating on – or at least fire up an electric heater if you’re still holding out on the radiators.
But while you were drawn to the indoor pleasures of heaters, hot casseroles and hotter coffee, you’ve also had your eye on party season, or at least been thinking about venturing into those corners of your wardrobe that haven’t seen daylight since March. From a clothes steamer to breathe new life into your threads, a pencil skirt and sheer silk shirt to update your wardrobe, to a vitamin C serum to keep your skin glowing all winter, these were your favourite things in October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: From a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right now

articles.author: Alex Curmi
articles.description:
Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself
Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round!”
It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. articles.description:
Liquid Static Studio; PC
You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.
Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there.

An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude
In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.
“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.
